subject: Specifying prior distribution parameters for standard deviation

messages.author: e1af1b5e367974aa
messages.subject: Specifying prior distribution parameters for standard deviation
parts:
Hello all,

I am trying to specify a prior for the standard deviation of the weight among individuals.

I've been looking into a lognormal distribution for this prior. Suppose I want to represent my beliefs that the SD is 20, should I specify my lognormal prior with parameters mu and sigma such that the peak of the distribution is centred at 20 (mu=log(20)) or such that the expected value of the distribution is 20 (mu=log(20)-.5*sigma^2).

How should I be thinking about this?

Thanks,

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Specifying prior distribution parameters for standard deviation
parts:
See: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations

The prior beliefs have to be a distribution, not a point
estimate.

I wouldn't worry too much about the asymmetry in lognormal, but
rather think about something like where you want 90% of the mass
in terms of an interval and construct the prior to do that.

- Bob

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Specifying prior distribution parameters for standard deviation
parts:
Just chiming in to clarify Ghislain's question, which was motivated by a discussion/disagreement we had the other day.

When designing the prior for a variability parameter, I might consider some value X as the most credible value for that parameter, with values above or below X relatively less credible, going to zero credibility at zero and positive infinity. For this scenario, I consider a lognormal to be a useful shape insofar as you can define where its peak is, how rapidly the credibility falls off away from this peak, and it's positive-bounded. 

I believe that, to reflect that I have maximum credibility at X, I'd want a lognormal peaked at X (so, in stan, "lognormal(log(X),...)" ). 

Ghislain notes that the expected mean of lognormal(log(X),Z) is exp(X+(Z^2)/2), and believes that if we want to reflect maximum credibility at X we'd need to set the mean and sd of the lognormal to yield an expected mean of X, not exp(X+(Z^2)/2) as the approach I suggest yields. 

Which of us (if either!) is correct?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Specifying prior distribution parameters for standard deviation
parts:
The positive boundedness and shape of tails (and head near zero)
are all worth thinking about. The peak isn't important, but
the probability mass in intervals is important.

Work backwards from what the prior does to your posterior
estimate. Individual points have measure zero and all the
Bayesian quantities of interest are expectations of functions of
parameters and involve posterior expectation calculations:

E[f(theta) | y] = INTEGRAL_theta f(theta) p(theta | y) d.theta

For example, event probabilities conditioned on the data
take f as an indicator function.

Pr[theta[1] > 0] = INTEGRAL_theta I[theta[1] > 0] p(theta | y) d.theta

The posterior breaks down as

p(theta | y) propto p(y | theta) * p(theta)

So this is where the prior p(theta) comes into the calculation---through
its affect on the posterior, and the only thing that matters is
the integrals over p(theta | y), not its peaks.

That's why you want to think in terms of interval probabilities,
not in terms of where the mode is. If you reparameterize, the
location of the mode may change without affecting the expectations.

- Bob
